questions.question: The mass $m$ of an object is graphed against the velocity $v$ of its motion. Which of the following graphs shows $\dfrac{dm}{dv}<0$ and $\dfrac{d^2m}{dv^2}=0$?
questions.answer: $\frac{dm}{dv}<0$ means $m$ is decreasing, and $\frac{d^2m}{dv^2}=0$ means the gradient is constant (no concavity), so the graph is a straight line with negative gradient: D. (A is decreasing but concave up; B is increasing; C is increasing.)

questions.question: Consider the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x-5}-5$. What is the equation of the horizontal asymptote?
questions.answer: As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\frac1{x-5}\to0$, so $y\to-5$. The horizontal asymptote is $y=-5$ (the vertical asymptote is $x=5$).

questions.question: Consider the function $f(x)=\sqrt{5-x}+\ln(2x+1)$. The domain of the function is:
questions.answer: $\sqrt{5-x}$ needs $5-x\ge0$, so $x\le5$. $\ln(2x+1)$ needs $2x+1>0$, so $x>-\tfrac12$. The domain is $\left(-\tfrac12,5\right]$.

questions.question:
The table shows the function values of $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$.

| $x$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | 3 | 0 | 3 | 12 | 27 |
| $g(x)$ | 4 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 0 |

What is the value of $A$ if $f(g(A))=0$?
questions.answer: $f(g(A))=0$ requires $g(A)=0$ (from the table $f(0)=0$ is the only zero of $f$). $g(3)=0$, so $A=3$.

questions.question: A box contains 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green counters. Two counters are drawn without replacement. The value of $P(\text{red}\mid\text{not green})$ is:
questions.answer: Given that a counter is not green, it is one of $5+4=9$ non-green counters, of which $5$ are red, so $P(\text{red}\mid\text{not green})=\dfrac{5/12}{9/12}=\dfrac59$ (the same value applies to either draw, by symmetry).

questions.question: Given $f(1)=9$, $f'(1)=-8$, $g(1)=1$ and $g'(1)=6$, and $h(x)=x\,f[g(x)]$, then $h'(1)=$
questions.answer: By the product and chain rules, $h'(x)=f[g(x)]+x\,f'[g(x)]\,g'(x)$. At $x=1$: $h'(1)=f(1)+1\cdot f'(1)\cdot g'(1)=9+(-8)(6)=-39$.

questions.question: The curve $y=f(x)$ is graphed below. What is the equation of the curve $y=g(x)$, where $g(x)=f'(x)$?
questions.answer: The graph has amplitude $\tfrac12$, passes through the origin rising, and completes 3 cycles in $2\pi$ (period $\tfrac{2\pi}3$), so $f(x)=\tfrac12\sin3x$. Then $g(x)=f'(x)=\tfrac12\cdot3\cos3x=\tfrac32\cos3x$.

questions.question: Which of the following definite integrals has the largest value?
questions.answer: The integrands in A, B and D are odd functions ($x^5$, $2\sin x$, $e^x-e^{-x}$), so each integral over $[-1,1]$ is $0$. In C, $\int_{-1}^{1}x^4dx=2\left[\tfrac{x^5}5\right]_0^1=\tfrac25>0$, so C is largest.

questions.question: For the angle $\theta$, $\tan\theta=\dfrac9{40}$ and $\sin\theta<0$. What is the value of $\cos(90^\circ-\theta)+\cos(180^\circ+\theta)$?
questions.answer: $\tan\theta>0$ and $\sin\theta<0$, so $\theta$ is in the third quadrant, with $\sin\theta=-\tfrac9{41}$ and $\cos\theta=-\tfrac{40}{41}$ (hypotenuse $\sqrt{9^2+40^2}=41$). Then $\cos(90^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta=-\tfrac9{41}$ and $\cos(180^\circ+\theta)=-\cos\theta=\tfrac{40}{41}$. The sum is $\tfrac{31}{41}$.

questions.question: Solve the equation $7-\dfrac{2-3x}{2}=4$.
questions.answer: $$7-\frac{2-3x}2=4\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{2-3x}2=3\ \Rightarrow\ 2-3x=6\ \Rightarrow\ x=-\frac43.$$

questions.question: Find the first term of the series $-12-8-4+\cdots$ that is greater than $150$.
questions.answer:
Arithmetic with $a=-12$, $d=4$: $T_n=-12+4(n-1)=4n-16$. Need $4n-16>150$, so $n>41.5$, so $n=42$ and $T_{42}=4(42)-16=152$.

The first term greater than $150$ is $152$.

questions.question: The diagram shows the graph of $y=f'(x)$. Describe the feature of the curve $y=f(x)$ at $x=6$. Justify your feature mathematically.
questions.answer: At $x=6$ the graph of $y=f'(x)$ touches the $x$-axis, so $f'(6)=0$ (stationary point), but $f'(x)<0$ on both sides of $x=6$ (the graph of $f'$ is below the axis just before and just after $x=6$). So the gradient is negative on both sides and does not change sign: $f(x)$ is decreasing through $x=6$ and the stationary point is a **horizontal point of inflexion** (the concavity changes since $f'$ has a local maximum at $x=6$).

questions.question: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\sqrt{2x+1}$ at the point where $x=4$.
questions.answer:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\tfrac12(2x+1)^{-1/2}\cdot2=\dfrac1{\sqrt{2x+1}}$. At $x=4$: $y=\sqrt9=3$ and $m=\tfrac13$.

$y-3=\tfrac13(x-4)\ \Rightarrow\ 3y-9=x-4\ \Rightarrow\ x-3y+5=0$, i.e. $y=\tfrac13x+\tfrac53$.

questions.question: Solve the equation $|4-3x|=13$.
questions.answer:
$4-3x=13\Rightarrow x=-3$, or $4-3x=-13\Rightarrow3x=17\Rightarrow x=\tfrac{17}3$.

So $x=-3$ or $x=\tfrac{17}3$.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{x^2}{\sin x}\right)$.
questions.answer:
Quotient rule with $u=x^2$, $v=\sin x$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^2}{\sin x}\right)=\frac{\sin x\cdot2x-x^2\cos x}{\sin^2x}=\frac{2x\sin x-x^2\cos x}{\sin^2x}.$$

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(2^x\log_2x\right)$.
questions.answer:
Product rule with $\frac{d}{dx}(2^x)=2^x\ln2$ and $\frac{d}{dx}(\log_2x)=\frac1{x\ln2}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(2^x\log_2x\right)=2^x\cdot\frac1{x\ln2}+2^x\ln2\cdot\log_2x=\frac{2^x}{x\ln2}+2^x\ln2\,\log_2x.$$

questions.question: A particle moves along the $x$-axis with its displacement, in metres from $O$, at time $t$ seconds, given by $x=2t^2-\ln t$. Where and when does the particle come to rest?
questions.answer:
$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=4t-\dfrac1t$ (for $t>0$). At rest: $v=0\Rightarrow4t^2-1=0\Rightarrow(2t-1)(2t+1)=0$, so $t=\tfrac12$ (rejecting $t=-\tfrac12$ since $t>0$ for $\ln t$ to be defined).

At $t=\tfrac12$: $x=2\left(\tfrac12\right)^2-\ln\tfrac12=\tfrac12+\ln2$.

The particle is at rest at $t=\tfrac12$ s, when it is $\tfrac12+\ln2\approx1.19$ m from $O$.

questions.question: A triangular prism $ABCDEF$ is made as a door wedge. It has a height of $22$ mm and a width of $60$ mm. The angle of the wedge is $18^\circ$ (the angle $EAD$). Find the angle, correct to the nearest degree, between the diagonal $BE$ and the diagonal of the base $ABCD$ (the base is a rectangle with $AB=60$ mm, and $DE=22$ mm is perpendicular to the base).
questions.answer:
In $\triangle EDA$ (right angle at $D$): $\tan18^\circ=\dfrac{22}{AD}\Rightarrow AD=\dfrac{22}{\tan18^\circ}=67.71$ mm.

The base diagonal is $BD$: $BD=\sqrt{60^2+67.71^2}=90.47$ mm.

$E$ is directly above $D$, so the angle between $BE$ and the base diagonal $BD$ is $\angle EBD$ in right triangle $EDB$:
$$\tan\theta=\frac{22}{90.47}\Rightarrow\theta=13.7^\circ\approx14^\circ.$$

questions.question: Solve the equation $2\log_75=2\log_7x-\log_73$.
questions.answer: $\log_7 25=\log_7\dfrac{x^2}3\Rightarrow25=\dfrac{x^2}3\Rightarrow x^2=75$. Since $x>0$ (for $\log_7x$), $x=\sqrt{75}=5\sqrt3$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int(\ln3)\,x^2\,dx$.
questions.answer: $\ln3$ is a constant, so $\displaystyle\int(\ln3)x^2dx=\frac{(\ln3)\,x^3}{3}+C$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{3x}{3-x^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
The derivative of $3-x^2$ is $-2x$, so $3x=-\tfrac32\cdot(-2x)$:
$$\int\frac{3x}{3-x^2}dx=-\frac32\int\frac{-2x}{3-x^2}dx=-\frac32\ln\left|3-x^2\right|+C.$$

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{2}\frac{dx}{(4-x)^2}$.
Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2-6\right)^8$.
questions.answer: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^2-6\right)^8=8\left(x^2-6\right)^7\cdot2x=16x\left(x^2-6\right)^7.$$

questions.question: Using the result $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^2-6\right)^8=16x\left(x^2-6\right)^7$, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2x\left(x^2-6\right)^7dx$.
questions.answer:
$$\int_0^2x(x^2-6)^7dx=\frac1{16}\int_0^216x(x^2-6)^7dx=\frac1{16}\left[(x^2-6)^8\right]_0^2=\frac1{16}\left[(-2)^8-(-6)^8\right]$$
$$=\frac{256-1\,679\,616}{16}=-104\,960.$$

*Note: the school's solution gives $104\,992$, which has the wrong sign and a slip in the arithmetic; the correct value is $-104\,960$ (the integrand is negative on $[0,2]$ since $x^2-6<0$ so $(x^2-6)^7<0$).*

questions.question: Prove that $$\frac{\sin\theta}{1+\cos\theta}+\frac{1+\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta.$$
questions.answer:
$$\text{LHS}=\frac{\sin^2\theta+(1+\cos\theta)^2}{(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta}=\frac{\sin^2\theta+1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta}{(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta}$$
Using $\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1$:
$$=\frac{2+2\cos\theta}{(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta}=\frac{2(1+\cos\theta)}{(1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta}=\frac2{\sin\theta}=2\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\text{RHS}.$$

questions.question:
The random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution:

| $x$ | 2 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X=x)$ | $\tfrac16$ | $\tfrac13$ | $\tfrac14$ | $p$ | $q$ |

Find the values of $p$ and $q$, given $P(X=\{\text{prime}\cap\text{odd}\})=\dfrac{31}{48}$.
questions.answer:
The probabilities sum to 1: $\tfrac16+\tfrac13+\tfrac14+p+q=1\Rightarrow p+q=\tfrac14$.

The odd primes in the table are $3,5,7$, so $P(\text{prime}\cap\text{odd})=\tfrac13+\tfrac14+p=\tfrac{31}{48}\Rightarrow p=\tfrac{31}{48}-\tfrac{28}{48}=\tfrac1{16}$.

Then $q=\tfrac14-\tfrac1{16}=\tfrac3{16}$.

questions.question:
The random variable $X$ has the following probability distribution:

| $x$ | 2 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $P(X=x)$ | $\tfrac16$ | $\tfrac13$ | $\tfrac14$ | $\tfrac1{16}$ | $\tfrac3{16}$ |

Find $E(X)$.
questions.answer: $$E(X)=\sum xP(x)=\frac26+\frac33+\frac54+\frac7{16}+\frac{27}{16}=\frac{113}{24}\approx4.71.$$

questions.question: The graph of $y=\sqrt x$ has been dilated both horizontally and vertically by a factor of $2$ and then translated to the left $3$ units before being reflected in the $x$-axis, to produce the equation $y=g(x)$. Write down the equation of $y=g(x)$.
questions.answer:
Dilation by a factor of 2 horizontally and vertically: replace $x$ by $\tfrac x2$ and $y$ by $\tfrac y2$: $\tfrac y2=\sqrt{\tfrac x2}$, i.e. $y=2\sqrt{\tfrac x2}$.

Translate 3 units left: replace $x$ by $x+3$: $y=2\sqrt{\tfrac{x+3}2}$.

Reflect in the $x$-axis (replace $y$ by $-y$):
$$y=g(x)=-2\sqrt{\frac{x+3}2}.$$

questions.question:
Two mountains, $P$ and $Q$, lie directly north of a campground $C$. Rehan walks from $C$ on a bearing of $065^\circ$ to a point $T$, a distance of $4$ km. The diagram shows the relative positions, viewed from above (not to scale). From $T$, the base of mountain $P$ is on a bearing of $285^\circ$ and the base of mountain $Q$ is on a bearing of $315^\circ$.

Explain why $\angle QTC=70^\circ$.
questions.answer:
The bearing of $C$ from $T$ is $065^\circ+180^\circ=245^\circ$ (the back bearing, using co-interior angles with the north lines). The bearing of $Q$ from $T$ is $315^\circ$, so $\angle QTC=315^\circ-245^\circ=70^\circ$.

(Alternatively: $\angle PTQ=315^\circ-285^\circ=30^\circ$ and $\angle CTP=285^\circ-245^\circ=40^\circ$, so $\angle QTC=30^\circ+40^\circ=70^\circ$.)

questions.question:
Two mountains, $P$ and $Q$, lie directly north of a campground $C$. Rehan walks from $C$ on a bearing of $065^\circ$ to a point $T$, a distance of $4$ km. The diagram shows the relative positions, viewed from above (not to scale). From $T$, the base of mountain $P$ is on a bearing of $285^\circ$ and the base of mountain $Q$ is on a bearing of $315^\circ$.

Given $\angle QTC=70^\circ$, find the distance $CQ$, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.answer:
In $\triangle CQT$: $\angle QCT=65^\circ$, $\angle QTC=70^\circ$, so $\angle CQT=180^\circ-65^\circ-70^\circ=45^\circ$. By the sine rule:
$$\frac{CQ}{\sin70^\circ}=\frac4{\sin45^\circ}\Rightarrow CQ=\frac{4\sin70^\circ}{\sin45^\circ}=5.3\text{ km (1 d.p.)}.$$

questions.question:
Two mountains, $P$ and $Q$, lie directly north of a campground $C$. Rehan walks from $C$ on a bearing of $065^\circ$ to a point $T$, a distance of $4$ km. The diagram shows the relative positions, viewed from above (not to scale). From $T$, the base of mountain $P$ is on a bearing of $285^\circ$ and the base of mountain $Q$ is on a bearing of $315^\circ$.

Given that $CQ=5.3157$ km (unrounded), find the distance $PQ$.
questions.answer:
In $\triangle CPT$: $\angle PCT=65^\circ$, $\angle CTP=40^\circ$, so $\angle CPT=75^\circ$. By the sine rule:
$$\frac{CP}{\sin40^\circ}=\frac4{\sin75^\circ}\Rightarrow CP=\frac{4\sin40^\circ}{\sin75^\circ}=2.662\text{ km}.$$
$$PQ=CQ-CP=5.316-2.662=2.65\approx2.7\text{ km}.$$

*Note: the school's solution subtracts the already-rounded values ($5.3-2.7$) and gets $2.6$ km; using unrounded values gives $2.65\ldots\approx2.7$ km.*

questions.question:
Thomas makes up a card game where he gets points for the type of card chosen randomly from a well-shuffled deck of 52 playing cards. He replaces the card chosen after each draw. The game is scored as follows:

- He scores $10$ points if he draws an Ace, King, Queen or Jack.
- He scores $3$ points if he draws a card less than $10$ (2 to 9).
- He scores $-10$ points if the card drawn is a $10$ of any suit.

What is the probability that Thomas will score zero in his first 2 draws?
questions.answer:
There are $16$ picture cards/aces ($+10$), $32$ cards from 2 to 9 ($+3$) and $4$ tens ($-10$). A total of zero after two draws is only possible with $+10$ and $-10$ (in either order), since $3+3=6$, $3-10=-7$, $3+10=13$, etc. are non-zero:
$$P=\frac{16}{52}\times\frac4{52}+\frac4{52}\times\frac{16}{52}=\frac{128}{2704}=\frac8{169}.$$

questions.question: Thomas plays a card game with a well-shuffled deck of 52 playing cards, replacing the card after each draw. His rules are: he wins and the game stops if he draws an Ace, King, Queen or Jack; he plays again if he draws a card less than $10$ (2 to 9); he loses and the game stops if he draws a $10$ of any suit. What is the probability that he wins the game?
questions.answer:
$P(\text{win on a draw})=\tfrac{16}{52}$, $P(\text{play again})=\tfrac{32}{52}$. He wins on draw 1, or after one replay then wins, etc.:
$$P(W)=\frac{16}{52}+\frac{32}{52}\cdot\frac{16}{52}+\left(\frac{32}{52}\right)^2\frac{16}{52}+\cdots=\frac{16}{52}\left(1+\frac{32}{52}+\left(\frac{32}{52}\right)^2+\cdots\right)$$
This is a geometric series with $a=1$, $r=\tfrac{32}{52}$, $|r|<1$, so $S_\infty=\dfrac1{1-\frac{32}{52}}=\dfrac{52}{20}$:
$$P(W)=\frac{16}{52}\times\frac{52}{20}=\frac45.$$
(Alternatively, only a winning or losing card ends the game, so $P(W)=\frac{16}{16+4}=\frac45$.)

questions.question: A sector $OPQ$ of a circle is shown in the diagram. The circle has its centre at $O$ and a radius of $8$ cm, and $\angle QOP=\dfrac\pi6$. Find the perimeter of the shaded segment (bounded by the chord $PQ$ and the arc $PQ$), leaving your answer in exact form.
questions.answer:
Chord $PQ$ (cosine rule in $\triangle OPQ$ with $OP=OQ=8$):
$$PQ^2=8^2+8^2-2(8)(8)\cos\tfrac\pi6=128-128\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}2=128-64\sqrt3,$$
so $PQ=\sqrt{128-64\sqrt3}$ (which equals $8\sqrt{2-\sqrt3}$).

Arc $PQ$: $l=r\theta=8\times\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac{4\pi}3$.

$$\text{Perimeter}=\frac{4\pi}3+\sqrt{128-64\sqrt3}\ \text{cm}.$$

questions.question: Mathsville's population at the start of 2000 is unknown. However, by the beginning of 2020 it had grown to $2.5$ million. Assuming that the population of Mathsville can be modelled exponentially using the equation $P=Ae^{0.0144t}$, where $A$ is a constant and $t$ is measured in years from the beginning of 2000, find the value of $A$.
questions.answer:
The beginning of 2020 is $t=20$, with $P=2.5\times10^6$:
$$2.5\times10^6=Ae^{0.0144\times20}=Ae^{0.288}\Rightarrow A=\frac{2.5\times10^6}{e^{0.288}}\approx1\,874\,404.$$

*Note: the school's solution uses $t=10$ (giving $A\approx2\,164\,719$), but 2000 to 2020 is 20 years. The conclusion in part (ii) is the same either way.*

questions.question: The population of Mathsville is modelled by $P=Ae^{0.0144t}$, where $t$ is measured in years from the beginning of 2000 and $A\approx1\,874\,404$ (the population was $2.5$ million at the beginning of 2020). A newspaper article, published in 1980, forecast that the population of Mathsville would reach $5$ million by the year $2050$. Using calculations to justify your response, state whether you agree or disagree with this article.
questions.answer:
At the year 2050, $t=50$:
$$P=1\,874\,404\times e^{0.0144\times50}=1\,874\,404\times e^{0.72}\approx3.85\text{ million}.$$
(Equivalently $P=2.5\times10^6\times e^{0.0144\times30}\approx3.85$ million.)

The model predicts about $3.85$ million, which is less than $5$ million, so I **disagree** with the newspaper article's forecast.

questions.question: For the curve $f(x)=x^4-8x^2$, show that $y=f(x)$ represents an even function.
questions.answer: $f(-x)=(-x)^4-8(-x)^2=x^4-8x^2=f(x)$, so $f$ is an even function.

questions.question: For the curve $f(x)=x^4-8x^2$, find the coordinates of all the stationary points and determine their nature.
questions.answer:
$f'(x)=4x^3-16x=4x(x^2-4)=4x(x+2)(x-2)=0\Rightarrow x=0,\pm2$.

$f(0)=0$ and $f(\pm2)=16-32=-16$. The stationary points are $(0,0)$, $(-2,-16)$ and $(2,-16)$.

Nature (using $f''(x)=12x^2-16$): $f''(0)=-16<0$, so $(0,0)$ is a local maximum; $f''(\pm2)=32>0$, so $(-2,-16)$ and $(2,-16)$ are local minima. (Equivalently, a table of the sign of $f'(x)$: for $x=-3,-2,-1$: $f'=-60,0,12$, i.e. $\searrow$ then $\nearrow$; for $x=-1,0,1$: $12,0,-12$, i.e. $\nearrow$ then $\searrow$; for $x=1,2,3$: $-12,0,60$.)

questions.question: For the curve $f(x)=x^4-8x^2$, find any points of inflexion.
questions.answer:
$f''(x)=12x^2-16=0\Rightarrow x^2=\tfrac43\Rightarrow x=\pm\dfrac2{\sqrt3}$.

Check that the concavity changes: $f''(-3)=92>0$, $f''(-1)=-4<0$, $f''(1)=-4<0$, $f''(3)=92>0$, so $f''$ changes sign at each of these values.

$y=\left(\tfrac43\right)^2-8\left(\tfrac43\right)=\tfrac{16}9-\tfrac{96}9=-\tfrac{80}9$. The points of inflexion are $\left(\pm\dfrac2{\sqrt3},-\dfrac{80}9\right)$.

questions.question: Sketch the curve $f(x)=x^4-8x^2$ in the domain showing all stationary points as well as any inflexions and intercepts with the coordinate axes. (Use: $f$ is even; stationary points $(0,0)$ maximum and $(\pm2,-16)$ minima; inflexions at $\left(\pm\tfrac2{\sqrt3},-\tfrac{80}9\right)$.)
questions.answer:
Intercepts: $y$-intercept $(0,0)$; $x$-intercepts from $x^2(x^2-8)=0$: $x=0$ and $x=\pm\sqrt8=\pm2\sqrt2$.

The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis (even), rises steeply as $|x|\to\infty$, has a local maximum at the origin, local minima at $(\pm2,-16)$ and inflexions at $\left(\pm\tfrac2{\sqrt3},-\tfrac{80}9\right)$ (on the way down from the origin to the minima). Marks: even symmetry; all stationary and inflexion points correct; intercepts on the $x$-axis correct.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\frac{\cos^2\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)}{\cos^2x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Since $\cos\left(\tfrac\pi2-x\right)=\sin x$, the integrand is $\dfrac{\sin^2x}{\cos^2x}=\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$:
$$\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}(\sec^2x-1)dx=\Big[\tan x-x\Big]_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}=\left(\sqrt3-\frac\pi3\right)-\left(1-\frac\pi4\right)=\sqrt3-1-\frac\pi{12}.$$

questions.question:
Jerome starts working on January 1, 2027. The advertised wage is \$56 000 p.a. After the first year his wage will increase to \$62 000, then increase by the same amount each year for the first 10 years of his employment; after that it will increase by the CPI of 3% p.a.

Show that Jerome earns \$74 000 at the start of 2030.
questions.answer: The wage forms an arithmetic sequence with $a=56\,000$ and $d=62\,000-56\,000=6000$. The start of 2030 is the 4th year: $T_4=56\,000+3(6000)=\$74\,000$.

questions.question: Jerome's wage is \$56 000 in his first year and increases by \$6000 each year for the first 10 years of his employment. How much will Jerome earn in total for the first 10 years?

Jerome's wage is \$56 000 in his first year and increases by \$6000 each year for the first 10 years (he earns \$830 000 in total over these 10 years). After that his wage increases by the CPI of 3% p.a. How many years will Jerome need to work before the total he has earned is over 2 million dollars?
questions.answer:
In year 10 his wage is $56\,000+9(6000)=\$110\,000$, so in year 11 it is $110\,000\times1.03=\$113\,300$. From year 11, the wages form a geometric series with $a=113\,300$ and $r=1.03$. After a further $n$ years:
$$830\,000+\frac{113\,300\left(1.03^n-1\right)}{0.03}>2\,000\,000\Rightarrow1.03^n-1>\frac{1\,170\,000\times0.03}{113\,300}=0.30979\ldots$$
$$1.03^n>1.3098\Rightarrow n>\frac{\ln1.3098}{\ln1.03}=9.13\ldots$$
So $n=10$ further years, and Jerome must work $10+10=\mathbf{20}$ years.

questions.question: The graphs of $y=\sin2x$ and $y=\cos x$ in the domain $-\dfrac\pi2\le x\le\pi$ are shown. Show that the coordinates of the point $A$, the point of intersection of the two curves in the first quadrant, is $\left(\dfrac\pi6,\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.
questions.answer:
The curves intersect where $\sin2x=\cos x$:
$$2\sin x\cos x=\cos x\Rightarrow\cos x(2\sin x-1)=0\Rightarrow\cos x=0\text{ or }\sin x=\tfrac12.$$
In the first quadrant ($0<x<\tfrac\pi2$), $\cos x\ne0$, so $\sin x=\tfrac12$ and $x=\tfrac\pi6$. Then $y=\cos\tfrac\pi6=\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$, so $A=\left(\tfrac\pi6,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.

questions.question: The graphs of $y=\sin2x$ and $y=\cos x$ in the domain $-\dfrac\pi2\le x\le\pi$ are shown, and they meet at $x=-\tfrac\pi2$, $x=\tfrac\pi6$ and $x=\tfrac\pi2$. Find the shaded area (the region enclosed between the two curves from $x=-\tfrac\pi2$ to $x=\tfrac\pi2$).
questions.answer:
For $-\tfrac\pi2\le x\le\tfrac\pi6$, $\cos x\ge\sin2x$; for $\tfrac\pi6\le x\le\tfrac\pi2$, $\sin2x\ge\cos x$.
$$A=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}(\cos x-\sin2x)dx+\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}(\sin2x-\cos x)dx$$
$$=\left[\sin x+\tfrac12\cos2x\right]_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}+\left[-\tfrac12\cos2x-\sin x\right]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}$$
First part: $\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac14\right)-\left(-1-\tfrac12\right)=\tfrac34+\tfrac32=\tfrac94$.

Second part: $\left(\tfrac12-1\right)-\left(-\tfrac14-\tfrac12\right)=-\tfrac12+\tfrac34=\tfrac14$.

$$A=\tfrac94+\tfrac14=\tfrac52\text{ square units}.$$

questions.question: A point $P(x,f(x))$ lies on the curve $f(x)=\dfrac2{\sqrt[5]{e^x}}=2e^{-x/5}$. The perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis, at $Q$, is shown and triangle $OPQ$ is shaded. Find the area of triangle $OPQ$ in terms of $x$.
questions.answer:
$OQ=x$ and $PQ=f(x)=2e^{-x/5}$, so
$$A=\tfrac12\times x\times2e^{-x/5}=xe^{-x/5}.$$

questions.question: A point $P(x,f(x))$ lies on the curve $f(x)=2e^{-x/5}$ and $Q$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the $x$-axis. The area of triangle $OPQ$ is $A=xe^{-x/5}$ ($x>0$). Find the $x$-coordinate of $P$ for which the triangle $OPQ$ has a maximum area.
questions.answer:
By the product rule, $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=e^{-x/5}+x\left(-\tfrac15\right)e^{-x/5}=e^{-x/5}\left(1-\dfrac x5\right)$.

$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0\Rightarrow1-\dfrac x5=0\Rightarrow x=5$ (since $e^{-x/5}\ne0$).

Nature: $e^{-x/5}>0$ for all $x$, so the sign of $\frac{dA}{dx}$ is that of $1-\frac x5$: at $x=4$ it is $+$, at $x=5$ it is $0$, at $x=6$ it is $-$. So $A$ has a maximum at $x=5$.

questions.question: The curve $y=f(x)=2e^{-x/5}$ crosses the $y$-axis at $S$, and $T$ is the point on the curve where $y=\tfrac12$. Find the exact value of $x$ at the point $T$.
questions.answer: $2e^{-x/5}=\tfrac12\Rightarrow e^{-x/5}=\tfrac14\Rightarrow-\tfrac x5=\ln\tfrac14=-\ln4\Rightarrow x=5\ln4$ ($=10\ln2$).

questions.question: The curve $y=f(x)=2e^{-x/5}$ crosses the $y$-axis at $S(0,2)$, and $T$ is the point on the curve with $y=\tfrac12$, at $x=5\ln4$. Find the area of the shaded region, between the line $ST$ and the curve $y=f(x)$.
questions.answer:
The line $ST$ lies above the (concave up) curve between $S$ and $T$, so the shaded area is the area of the trapezium under $ST$ minus the area under the curve.

Trapezium: $\tfrac12\left(2+\tfrac12\right)\times5\ln4=\tfrac54\times5\ln4=\tfrac{25}4\ln4=\tfrac{25}2\ln2$.

Area under the curve: $\displaystyle\int_0^{5\ln4}2e^{-x/5}dx=\left[-10e^{-x/5}\right]_0^{5\ln4}=-10\cdot\tfrac14+10=\tfrac{15}2$.

$$\text{Shaded area}=\frac{25}2\ln2-\frac{15}2=\frac12\left(25\ln2-15\right)\text{ square units}.$$
